blocks.prompt: Every Part Has a Job
blocks.text: A car is made of many parts, and each part has a job. The wheels turn so the car can roll. Each wheel has a rubber tire full of air. The air makes the ride soft and helps bumpy roads feel smoother. Under the hood sits the engine. It burns fuel and turns the wheels. The steering wheel turns the front wheels left or right. The brakes squeeze the wheels and slow them down. The lights let the driver see at night, and let other people see the car. Every part is doing one small job. Together they get you home.

blocks.prompt: Two Machines in One Car
blocks.text: Push a toy car and it rolls, then stops. A real car carries its own push around with it. That push comes from the engine. Gasoline holds a lot of energy locked inside it. Inside the engine are metal tubes called cylinders. A tiny spray of gasoline mixes with air inside a cylinder. A spark sets it off, and the mixture burns in a fast puff. The puff shoves a piston down the tube. In each cylinder that happens dozens of times every second, and all those little shoves add up into spinning. The spinning travels down a shaft, out to the wheels, and the car moves. Stopping works the opposite way. When the driver presses the brake pedal, pads squeeze against a metal disc on each wheel. The rubbing turns the car's motion into heat. Brake discs on a race car can glow red. So a car is really two machines in one. One makes motion out of fuel. The other turns motion back into heat when you want to stop.

blocks.prompt: The Woman Who Took the First Car
blocks.text: In 1886, Karl Benz patented a machine that nobody wanted. It had three wheels, a bench seat, and a small engine that popped and rattled. Benz called it the Patent-Motorwagen. People called it a nuisance. Benz was a careful man, and he kept tinkering instead of selling. His wife, Bertha Benz, had paid for much of the work with her own money. She decided the machine needed proof, not more tinkering. One morning in August 1888, before her husband woke up, she pushed the car out of the workshop with her two teenage sons and drove it about 66 miles to visit her mother in Pforzheim. She left a note. Nothing about the trip was easy. There were no gas stations, because there were no cars. When the tank ran low she stopped at a pharmacy in Wiesloch and bought a cleaning fluid called ligroin, which is why that pharmacy is remembered today as the world's first filling station. When the fuel line clogged, she cleared it with her hat pin. When a wire wore bare, she wrapped it with a garter. When the wooden brake blocks gave out on the hills, she found a shoemaker and had him nail leather over them, inventing brake linings on the spot. She arrived at dusk and sent her husband a telegram. Newspapers picked up the story. Suddenly the machine was not a nuisance. It was a thing that could carry you 66 miles. Bertha Benz never held a patent. She held the steering tiller.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Nikolaus Otto worked out the four-stroke cycle in 1876
Suck, squeeze, bang, blow
A gasoline engine wastes about three quarters of its fuel as heat
Electric motors deliver about ninety percent as motion

blocks.prompt: Most of Your Gas Never Moves the Car
blocks.text: Fill a car's tank with gasoline and you are buying energy. Roughly three quarters of it will never move the car an inch. Here is where it goes. A gasoline engine runs on a cycle worked out by Nikolaus Otto in 1876, and it repeats four steps over and over in every cylinder. Intake: a piston slides down and pulls in a mist of fuel and air. Compression: the piston rises and squeezes that mist into a space the size of a thimble. Power: a spark ignites it, the mixture burns, and the sudden expansion drives the piston back down. Exhaust: the piston rises again and pushes the burnt gas out. Suck, squeeze, bang, blow, as mechanics say. Only the third step does any work. Burning fuel makes heat, and heat is a clumsy way to make motion. Most of the heat pours straight out of the tailpipe or soaks into the metal of the engine, which is why a car needs a radiator, a fan, and a couple of gallons of coolant just to keep from cooking itself. A typical gasoline engine converts about a quarter of the energy in its fuel into turning the wheels. The rest is warm air. An electric motor does not burn anything. It uses a magnetic field to pull a shaft around, and it delivers around ninety percent of the electricity it draws as motion. It can also run backwards. Take your foot off the pedal and the motor becomes a generator, slowing the car and pushing charge back into the battery, so some braking energy is recovered instead of thrown away as brake heat. None of this makes electric cars free of cost. The electricity has to be generated somewhere, and building a battery takes mining, energy, and water. But the comparison is worth understanding clearly. The gasoline engine is a remarkable machine that spent a century getting better at a job that is thermodynamically hard. The electric motor is a simpler machine doing an easier job.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Machine That Carries Its Own Push

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ford's moving line cut Model T chassis time from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes
The Model T fell from about 850 dollars to under 300
Leaded gasoline sold in the US from 1923 until 1996
The last country stopped selling it in 2021
Volvo gave away the three-point seat belt patent in 1959
Nils Bohlin designed fighter ejection seats before seat belts

blocks.prompt: Four Decisions Inside Every Car
blocks.text: A car looks like one invention. It is not. It is a stack of decisions, made by different people, in different centuries, for different reasons, and you are sitting inside all of them at once. Four of those decisions are worth knowing. The first was about speed of building. In 1913, at Ford's Highland Park plant, engineers stopped moving workers to the car and started moving the car to the workers. A chassis crawled along a rope-drawn line while each person did one small task, over and over. The time to assemble a Model T chassis fell from around twelve hours to about ninety minutes. The price fell with it, from around 850 dollars at launch to under 300, and a machine that had been a rich man's toy became something a factory worker could own. The same decision made the work numbingly repetitive. Ford had to double wages to five dollars a day just to keep anyone on the line. Cheapness and boredom arrived together, and they were the same decision. The second was about knock. Early engines pinged and hammered when the fuel ignited too early, which limited how hard they could be pushed. In 1921 a General Motors engineer named Thomas Midgley Jr. found that adding a lead compound to gasoline stopped the knock cleanly. It worked. It was also poison, and people knew it was poison. Workers at the plants that made the additive hallucinated and died, and newspapers reported it at the time. Leaded gasoline sold anyway, for more than seventy years, and every car burning it sprayed lead into the air children breathed. The geochemist Clair Patterson, who was trying to measure the age of the Earth and kept finding lead contamination in everything he touched, spent decades forcing the truth into the open. The United States finished banning it for road cars in 1996. The last country stopped selling it in 2021. Midgley, who also invented the refrigerant gases that later tore a hole in the ozone layer, may have harmed more of the atmosphere than any other single person, and he was trying to be helpful the whole time. The third was about crashing. Cars already had lap belts, which held your hips and let your head keep going. In 1959 a Volvo engineer named Nils Bohlin, who had spent his earlier career designing ejection seats for fighter pilots, worked out a belt that anchored at three points, held the chest and hips together, and could be fastened with one hand in one motion. Volvo then did something companies almost never do. It made the patent free for anyone to use, on the grounds that the invention was worth more to the world open than owned. Every three-point belt you have ever clicked shut descends from that choice. The fourth decision is yours, and it has not been made yet. It covers what a car should burn, where its battery metals come from, whether it should drive itself, and how much of a city should be paved over to park it. Every earlier decision in this list looked obvious to the people making it. Two of them were right. One of them poisoned a century. The people who put lead in gasoline were not villains in a story. They were engineers solving the problem directly in front of them, and they did not look far enough past it. That is the thing to carry out of this passage. A car is not a machine. It is an argument, still running.

(it reframes the car as an unfinished set of decisions the reader participates in; earned if the four examples show real choices with real consequences)
